hook.line: At the bank, Tomás asks for el señor Ruiz. When Mr Ruiz walks over, Tomás says "Buenos días, señor Ruiz." The little el disappears, and that's not a typo.
hook.es: El señor Ruiz está en el banco. —Buenos días, señor Ruiz.
hook.en: Mr Ruiz is at the bank. —Good morning, Mr Ruiz.

rule:
Señor and señora work like nouns, so they take el and la when you talk ABOUT someone:

El señor Ruiz trabaja en el banco.
La señora Gómez no está.

When you talk TO the person, the el or la drops:

Buenos días, señor Ruiz.
Señora Gómez, ¿usted habla inglés?

Don and doña are different. They go with a first name, they show warm respect (very Colombian), and they never take el or la, whether you talk to or about the person: Don Hernando llega. ¿Don Hernando, un tinto?

Plain names never take an article either: Vale trabaja aquí, not la Vale.
smallPrint: Señor and señora are titles that behave like common nouns, so they need the definite article in the third person.
soundTip: In señor the ñ is the ny in canyon: se-ÑOR.

pitfalls.why: When you speak to someone, señor stands alone.

pitfalls.wrong: Señor Ruiz trabaja en el banco.
pitfalls.right: El señor Ruiz trabaja en el banco.
pitfalls.why: Talking about him needs the el: el señor Ruiz.

pitfalls.wrong: El don Hernando llega a las siete.
pitfalls.right: Don Hernando llega a las siete.
pitfalls.why: Don and doña never take an article.

personal: Think of an older neighbour or colleague. Say one thing about them with el señor or la señora, then greet them directly.
